passage: I'm Parul, and I was in that chat, so I watched Vasudha. Someone posted a picture of Ananya's haircut, and the jokes started: one, then five, then ten laughing faces. Vasudha typed "lol she looks like a mop" almost straight away, faster than anyone. She's usually kind. In the corridor afterwards, she kept checking the chat, her smile stuck on her face. When Ananya walked by with her head down, Vasudha stared at the floor. I can't be certain, but she looked like she wanted to disappear. That evening I saw her typing for a long time in a private window with Ananya. Ananya later told me it said, "That was unkind. I'm sorry I joined in." I can't tell if Vasudha was scared of being next, but I think she was.

qa.q: What was the picture someone posted in the chat?
qa.a: It was a picture of Ananya's haircut.

qa.q: What might Vasudha have been feeling in the corridor, according to Parul?
qa.a: Uneasy and perhaps ashamed. She kept checking the chat with a stuck smile and stared at the floor when Ananya passed, though Parul is not sure.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do afterwards that helped?
qa.a: She sent Ananya a private message saying it was unkind and that she was sorry for joining in.

qa.q: How might Ananya have felt seeing the chat and then reading Vasudha's message?
qa.a: Hurt by the mocking and head-down in the corridor, and then perhaps somewhat comforted, at least, by a private apology.

grounding: Vasudha joins mocking a classmate in a group chat because everyone is laughing, and later sends the classmate a kind private message; a peer observes her.

passage:
Pooja, sit. You look worried about that group chat. Let me tell you something from when I was your age.
We didn't have phones, but we had a notebook that went round the back benches. One day someone drew a cartoon of Sebastian, the new boy, with huge ears and a joke about his old shirts. Everyone added something. When it came to me, I felt a flash of fear. If I didn't write something, would I be next?
So I wrote a joke. Everybody laughed. I felt big for one minute.
That evening I saw Sebastian at the bus stop, alone, rubbing his eyes. I felt sick. That was the turning point.
The next morning I tore that page out and gave it to him, along with a note: "I'm sorry I wrote on this. It was cruel. Want to sit with me at lunch?"
He did. He became one of my best friends. Your Francis Uncle still remembers how easy it was to be cruel.

qa.q: What did the back-bench notebook show about Sebastian?
qa.a: A cartoon with huge ears and a joke about his old shirts.

qa.q: Why did young Francis join in the mocking?
qa.a: He felt a flash of fear that if he didn't write something, he would be the next target.

qa.q: What was the turning point, and what did Francis do next?
qa.a: Seeing Sebastian alone at the bus stop made Francis feel sick; the next morning he tore out the page, apologised and invited Sebastian to lunch.

qa.q: How might Sebastian have felt seeing the notebook page?
qa.a: Sebastian likely felt humiliated and alone, being new and mocked by the whole back bench.

grounding: An elder recalls joining in mocking a new boy out of fear, noticing how easily he slid into cruelty, and apologising privately.

passage:
The wedding hall was loud, the network was patchy, and Keerthana's phone had eleven percent battery. She kept checking the class group anyway.
Someone had posted a clip of Hemant tripping on stage at the talent show. Everyone was adding laughing messages, nicknames, a meme. Keerthana laughed too and typed, "Hemant the ballet star." She sent it before thinking.
The group went wild. Her stomach twisted a second later. Last month, Hemant had helped her fix her bicycle chain in the rain. Why had she written that? Because everyone else was. Because she didn't want to be the only one silent, the next one in the clip.
With her phone on seven percent, she deleted her message. Then she wrote to Hemant privately: "I'm sorry for what I wrote. It was mean. You were brave to be up there at all."
Her phone died before she saw his answer. But she felt lighter all through the reception anyway.

qa.q: How much battery did Keerthana's phone have at first?
Why did Keerthana send the mean message?
qa.a: She felt a pull to fit in and a fear of being the next target, so she joined in without thinking.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do to stop her slide into cruelty?
qa.a: She deleted her message and privately apologised to Hemant, adding something kind about his courage.

qa.q: How might Hemant feel when he sees the group mocking him?
qa.a: Hemant probably feels humiliated and hurt, especially since he had been kind to Keerthana before.

grounding: A teen joins in mocking a classmate out of fear of being next, notices how easily she slid into cruelty, and sends a kind private message.
